"It's interesting because having been somewhat in that position where teams I was on, it's like, hey, at some point, your team continues to age, and you continue to get older, and it's like, when do you hold on?" Howard said. He cited the length of many of the core players’ contracts as an issue for the team because they are harder to move in a trade. Harper’s deal runs through 2031, Schwarber’s through 2030, Turner’s through 2033, Realmuto’s through 2028, Wheeler’s through 2027, Nola’s through 2030, Luzardo’s through 2031 and Sánchez’s through 2032. Compounding the Phillies’ problems, their farm system was ranked 26th in the sport by MLB.com, meaning there aren’t any immediate options to supplant struggling stars. Howard said something has to change for the Phillies, whether players are moved or not. "If you can't necessarily move people, then what you gotta do is, is you gotta change. To me, I think you got to change the philosophy and the dynamic inside the clubhouse. 'Cause if they're not going anywhere, then you've got to switch something up that you're doing internally. articles.title: Will Major League Baseball still lock players out after 2026 postseason proves owners wrong?
articles.summary: Major League Baseball's salary cap campaign takes a hit as four of the final five 2026 playoff teams rank in the bottom 11 in player payroll.
articles.body: Despite a number of fascinating storylines, much of the discussion during the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season was dominated by upcoming labor negotiations with the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement in December. The league office, essentially run by the 30 current owners, started an advertising and promotional campaign designed to inflame tensions and increase support for its proposed salary cap. As early as June, the league's official account made several posts telling fans how awful baseball is, while claiming that many fanbases have no "hope" of winning a World Series because of payroll disparities. "The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title," the first post said. "Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50." MLB OWNERS REVEAL NEW DETAILS OF SALARY CAP PROPOSAL THAT ALL BUT GUARANTEE A LOCKOUT THIS DECEMBER This was, of course, misleading; many teams get ancillary income that would not be included in the "50/50" split. And if the proposed floor would be achievable for the small market teams in 2027, it raises the question of why it wasn't in 2026. Even increased revenue sharing wouldn't come close to bridging the gap for most small market teams. Regardless though, that "hope" section, again posted in June, has taken a major, major blow by the results in the postseason. Because it turns out that while spending helps, it doesn't guarantee results. With the Dodgers, Brewers, and Tampa Bay Rays advancing to their respective league championship series on Wednesday, three of the four spots in the penultimate postseason round have been determined. The last spot will go to one of the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland Guardians. Five teams, out of 30, are left standing. And the Brewers will not be able to line up Jacob Misiorowski for two starts in the NLCS, including in Game 1 at American Family Field. Even if they do make it through the NLCS and the World Series, does the league really believe the message of "you have no hope" will resonate when four of the final five teams are in the bottom 11 in player payroll? Including the literal cheapest team in the sport, and coming off a series in which the No. 28 payroll team dominated the big spending Yankees in an easy 3-0 sweep? THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! These outcomes raise another key point; did Rays or White Sox fans realistically enter the season with "hope" of winning a World Series? Of course not. Chicago's just two seasons removed from one of the worst years in baseball history. The Rays did little this offseason to give fans reason for optimism. Yet here they are, favorites to advance through the American League for the second time in the past six years. Milwaukee fans might have lost hope when the front office traded Freddy Peralta to the Mets in the offseason...only for the Brewers to have an even better record in 2026, the best win-loss and run differential in the sport. With the 19th highest payroll. Point being, "hope" doesn't always relate to success. Mets fans started 2026 with "hope" after getting Peralta, Marcus Semien, Bo Bichette and Devin Williams. How'd that go? Yankees fans had hope with the exciting debut of Cam Schlittler in 2025, bringing back Cody Bellinger, and top prospects like Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr., reaching the big leagues. Their reward? A sweep from the Rays. Most small market teams have reached the LCS, many multiple times. Yes, the Dodgers have dominated, but the Mets have the same number of LCS appearances as Cleveland, Kansas City, and Tampa Bay. articles.title: What happened in viral video of Dodgers fan refusing ball to child? Incident explained
articles.summary: A Los Angeles Dodgers fan has sparked a heated debate after refusing to give a foul ball he caught during a playoff game to a young Atlanta Braves
articles.body: A Los Angeles Dodgers fan has sparked a heated debate after refusing to give a foul ball he caught during a playoff game to a young Atlanta Braves supporter sitting nearby. The fan, wearing a Yoshinobu Yamamoto jersey, was urged by other spectators to hand over the ball, but he refused. A video of the exchange shows the child looking disappointed as the adult keeps his catch. The incident has divided baseball fans, with some defending the man’s right to keep the souvenir and others questioning his decision.Dodgers fan refuses to give foul ball to young Braves supporterThe incident took place during Game 3 of the National League Division Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Atlanta Braves on October 6. A spectator recorded the moment after the Dodgers fan caught a foul ball at Truist Park in Atlanta.The person filming the exchange could be heard shouting, ‘Give it to the kid! Give it to the kid!’However, the fan was unwilling to part with the ball. He replied, ‘I’m sorry, I can’t! I’m not giving it to the kid! I feel bad, but I’m not giving it to the kid!’The camera then showed the young Braves supporter sitting a few rows behind him. The child appeared disappointed, and the video soon spread across social media, prompting a debate about whether adults should give baseballs they catch to children.Some fans argued that catching a ball is special for adults, too. One wrote, ‘Had a foul ball literally drop right in my lap. It’s sitting on the shelf with other memorabilia. Been to many games and never came close to a foul ball. Just because I’m an adult doesn’t mean it wasn’t special for me, too.’Another commented, ‘If you caught it fair and square I have no problem with you keeping the ball at all, honestly. Is it a nice gesture to give it to the kid? Sure, but you don’t HAVE to, anyone making them feel bad for it should stop.’A third fan added, ‘Kids aren’t special. If you genuinely caught it, it’s yours. The kids have way more time to catch one in the future.’Another supporter wrote, ‘You have true baseball fans who go their entire lives wanting to catch a baseball,’ adding that this was not about someone attending a game only because tickets were free.Dodgers fan debate recalls Phillies Karen incidentOther fans felt the man had missed a chance to make a child happy. One wrote, ‘You don’t have to, that’s true. But it is revealing of one’s character if they don’t, and it’s not revealing anything particularly positive.’Another said, ‘There’s obviously nothing “wrong” with keeping it. It’s just a little weird to not give it to a kid….’A third added, ‘Being a good person isn’t hard,’ arguing that the fan should be criticised for not giving away the ball.The argument recalls the incident involving a Philadelphia Phillies fan known online as ‘Phillies Karen’. Last year, she demanded that a young boy hand over a home run ball hit by Harrison Bader. The boy’s father eventually gave her the ball.Lincoln Feltwell, the boy involved, told NBC 10 Philadelphia, ‘I wasn’t very happy that we had to give it to her, but we can’t win. She was going to get it anyways.’Another incident involving a Chicago Cubs fan also drew criticism earlier this season. Footage appeared to show a man shoving a woman while trying to get a home run ball hit by Pete Crow-Armstrong at Wrigley Field in August.One social media user criticised the behaviour, writing, ‘Putting your hands on a girl over a ball in the stands is peak loser behavior.’The latest incident has renewed the debate over baseball etiquette, with fans split over whether sharing a prized catch with a child should be expected or left to personal choice.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Jose Ramirez and the Cleveland Guardians kept their season alive for the second straight game against the Chicago White Sox.
articles.body:
Jose Ramirez and the Cleveland Guardians kept their season alive for the second straight game against the Chicago White Sox.

The Guardians picked up a 9-5 victory in Game 4 at Rate Field to force the ALDS matchup to a series-deciding Game 5 on Saturday night in Cleveland.

Best Fits for Michael King and Casey Mize ⚾

Ramirez was the offensive catalyst for the Guardians with a home run and three RBI.

Cleveland's offense did all of its damage in the fifth and sixth innings.

Patrick Bailey's pinch-hit home run started the fifth-inning rally.

Ramirez followed shortly after with a two-run home run that briefly put the Guardians in the lead.

The White Sox answered immediately with two runs. Sam Antonacci was hit by a pitch with the bases loaded and Brenton Doyle drove in a run on a sacrifice fly.

Cleveland delivered the offensive hammer in the top of the sixth with six runs. Ramirez, Chase DeLauter and Jo Adell combined to drive in four runs on their respective singles during the sixth.

Cleveland's top bullpen arms kept the White Sox bats quiet for the most of the closing stretch.

Miguel Vargas homered off Cleveland closer Cade Smith in the ninth, a hit that forced the Guardians to use presumed Game 5 starter Gavin Williams to finish off the game.

The Guardians and White Sox will head back to Cleveland for Game 5 on Saturday night.

The winner of Saturday's Game 5 heads to Florida for Game 1 of the ALCS against the Tampa Bay Rays on Monday night.

articles.title: José Ramírez, just in time to save the Guardians' season, has rediscovered his MVP form in ALDS vs. White Sox
articles.summary: In Cleveland's two victories in Chicago, Ramirez went 4-for-9 with a double, a triple, a home run, a walk, a stolen base, four runs scored and five RBI.
articles.body:
CHICAGO — Even in the worst full season of his career, a true superstar can turn it on at any time.

José Ramírez is arguably one of the five best players in Major League Baseball. He had a down year by his standards in 2026, but the Cleveland Guardians couldn't have picked a better time for their best player to get hot. With their season on the line in Game 4 of the ALDS against the Chicago White Sox and an opportunity to send the series back to Cleveland for a winner-take-all Game 5, the Guardians' superman found his cape.

"That's a future Hall of Famer," outfielder Chase DeLauter said after Cleveland's 9-5 victory on Thursday in Chicago . "It's special."

Through the first two games of the ALDS, Ramírez didn't look like the player Cleveland knows him to be, going 0-for-6 with three strikeouts. His early-series struggles seemingly carried over from the final month of the regular season, which saw him put up a paltry .198/.237/.264 slashline with just one home run.

But Game 3 on Wednesday seemed to have unlocked something for the Guardians' superstar. In that one, Ramírez went 2-for-4 with a double, a triple and a stolen base. He took over the game with his bat, glove and his legs. Then Ramírez had even more in store for Game 4.

Just like in Game 3, the White Sox took the momentum early on Thursday, taking a 2-0 lead into the fifth inning and running Guardians starter Parker Messick out of the game after just 2 1/3 innings. But once catcher Patrick Bailey cut the lead in half with a solo shot, it was time for Ramírez to make his mark on the game.

"It's contagious to the team, like the way he plays the game, the energy, his at-bat quality," second baseman Travis Bazzana said postgame. "I mean, we saw him [in Game 3] manufacture a run by himself. He got on, stole some bases and then scored. So he can make the impact so fast, but he plays with such intention."

Prior to Ramírez's fifth-inning at-bat, it felt like a big swing was coming. He flew out in his first at-bat before a sharp lineout in his second. But he found the barrel on both, with exit velocities of 98.9 mph and 97.5 mph, respectively.

Ramírez made sure the third ball he put in play wouldn't be caught. The Guardians' third baseman launched a two-run blast to put Cleveland ahead 3-2 and injected some much-needed confidence into the visiting dugout.

While he doesn't typically show a lot of emotion, Ramírez was sure to fire up his dugout before rounding the bases.

"It's a special moment when you have that type of energy from the guys," he said postgame. "I had a particular conversation with Messick before that. I told him, 'I'm going to get this turned around for you,' and I was able to execute it. It was really special."

Said manager Stephen Vogt: "It was José Ramírez being José Ramírez in the playoffs. Bring in a fastball, [Jordan] Hicks with a great fastball, and Josy got to it. To step up, say there he goes again. And a big moment for him, big moment for us, and he doesn't show a lot of emotion, but he was pretty excited tonight."

Although Cleveland's lead didn't hold long, with Chicago scoring two more in the bottom of the fifth, Ramírez for the second straight day galvanized the Guardians' offense. That three-run outburst in the fifth inning was just an appetizer. The entreé was a monster, six-run sixth inning that made it 9-4 and broke the game open.

As part of that six-run sixth, Ramírez added an RBI single, giving him back-to-back multi-hit games. Since that 0-for-6 in the first two games of the ALDS, the Cleveland superstar is 4-for-9 in the second pair of games, with a double, a triple, a home run, a walk, a stolen base, four runs scored and five RBI.

"It just starts with him. Whether he's hot, whether he's cold, just having him in the lineup, it's that presence," DeLauter said. "When he comes out firing, has that energy, has cool, big swings like that — it just rallies us together."

The numbers will tell you that Ramírez has not been at his best for much of 2026 — he had surgery on the hamate bone in his left hand in June, after all — but you wouldn't know it by his confidence. The seven-time All-Star might not be tall, but he walks around like he's a giant. And that confidence can be felt by everyone around him.

For the Guardians to fight back from a 2-0 series deficit while in Chicago and get back to Cleveland for a chance to reach the ALCS, they needed the best version of Ramírez to show up. And with not a moment to spare, it appears that he has rediscovered his elite form.

Now Cleveland has an opportunity to become the first team since the 2017 New York Yankees to win three straight games in a best-of-five series after losing the first two. Heading back home with a superstar who has gotten hot, an offense that's rolling and a White Sox team that's on the ropes, the Guardians appear to have all the momentum.

"It's going to be crazy," Ramírez said of what he expects for Game 5. "It's going to be an incredible energy. For us, it's going to be the same mindset: Try to win the game, and enjoy the environment that's going to be at Progressive [Field]."

articles.title: Each MLB Team's Biggest Roster Hole to Fix in 2026-27 Offseason
articles.summary: For a lot of Major League Baseball teams, the to-do list for this offseason is a metaphorical mile long.
articles.body:
For a lot of Major League Baseball teams, the to-do list for this offseason is a metaphorical mile long.

But every team has one biggest roster hole that it knows it needs to address before the 2027 campaign begins—whenever that may be.

For some, it's a brand-new hole left by a player about to hit free agency. They might just need to somehow find the funds to keep that player from landing elsewhere.

For many clubs, though, the biggest problem on the horizon was also what held them back this season. They ought to be extra motivated to make sure it doesn't happen again.

Teams are presented in alphabetical order by location.

ARI | ATH | ATL | BAL | BOS | CHC | CIN | CLE | COL | CWS | DET | HOU | KC | LAA | LAD | MIA | MIL | MIN | NYM | NYY | PHI | PIT | SD | SEA | SF | STL | TB | TEX | TOR | WSH

Save for Ildemaro Vargas—who had a .557 OPS over his final 118 games—and backup catcher James McCann, the rest of the lineup regulars will be back in 2027. If Jordan Lawler can stay healthy, the Snakes ought to be in business on offense.

The starting rotation also looks to be in good shape—provided Corbin Burnes does not opt out of the four years left on his contract, which seems very unlikely. If nothing changes, it'll be Burnes, Eduardo Rodriguez, Merrill Kelly, Brandon Pfaadt and Ryne Nelson, with 2026 rookies Mitch Bratt, José Cabrera and Kohl Drake available for depth.

But the Diamondbacks sure do have a ton of relievers hitting free agency.

Of the seven who appeared in more than 15 games (each appearing in at least 45), only Juan Morillo and Brandyn Garcia are slated to return.

Granted, those two were the best of the seven. Justin Martínez should feature prominently in the 2027 bullpen after missing the first 4.5 months of this past season while recovering from Tommy John surgery. They'll need to add depth, though, and possibly a dedicated closer.

Biggest Roster Hole : Pitching in General

Luis Severino has a $22M player option and will most likely exercise it. Meanwhile, the A's hold a $15M club option for Jeffrey Springs, which they will presumably decline.

Regardless of how things shake out with those veteran arms, though, the A's have a ton of work to do if they're hoping to bounce back from allowing 937 runs this season. That's 127 more runs than the second-worst AL pitching staff.

Best of luck solving that problem while continuing to call West Sacramento their temporary home. Given the way balls soar out of Sutter Health Park during the summer, free agent pitchers are going to be reluctant to sign with the A's unless they overpay or it's more or less their only option.

They can trade for pitchers, though. They have to try to contend—especially after 81-81 was good enough to win the AL West this year.

Biggest Roster Hole : Shortstop/Left Field

After watching Atlanta go with openers Ray Kerr, Dylan Dodd and Ray Kerr again as its starting pitchers in consecutive postseason games, the starting rotation may well be the correct answer here.

However, they do still have a deep stable of options. Chris Sale will be back as the ace, with Grant Holmes, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López, Spencer Strider, AJ Smith-Shawver, Spencer Schwellenbach, JR Ritchie and maybe Didier Fuentes all in the mix for starting gigs.

The problem was simply that most of those guys had been injured.

Meanwhile, with versatile Mauricio Dubón heading to free agency, the Braves are looking at a pretty big hole at shortstop and left field.

Technically, they do still have Jurickson Profar for another year. Maybe he returns from his second PED suspension and makes an impact in left? Short of that, though, it's an all-you-can-eat buffet for Mike Yastrzemski in left and Jim Jarvis at short.

Even if they manage to re-sign Dubón, they'll need at least one other option in that LF/SS mix—probably a right-handed-hitting shortstop, with Yaz's left-handed bat starting in left against righties while that TBD SS typically starts against southpaws.

Trevor Rogers is going to be one of the five most coveted arms in free agency this winter. Re-signing him will neither be easy nor cheap.

Baltimore also already traded away Dean Kremer and will have to replace Chris Bassitt in the starting rotation.

That leaves the O's with Kyle Bradish, Shane Baz, Brandon Young and a whole lot of unknowns beyond that.

Cade Povich and Trey Gibson could both be in the mix after each making a handful of starts in 2026, but neither one has quite proven himself worthy yet. The same goes for southpaw Luis De León, who made a few relief appearances in the big leagues, but needs to work on his walk rate before he can start in the majors.

They also have three highly touted prospects in Anthony Eyanson, Joseph Dzierwa and Caden Hunter, but they haven't even pitched in Triple-A yet. They might still be at least a year away.

While they wait on those guys in their early 20s, maybe the Orioles can trade for one year of someone like Sandy Alcantara, Logan Gilbert or Joe Ryan.

Though it sounds like Sonny Gray is more likely to retire than return to the Red Sox in 2027, they still have a stout-looking rotation, thanks to the emergence of Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett. That duo should pair with Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez and Brayan Bello, with Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford also candidates for the 2027 rotation after missing most or all of 2026 to injury.

Rather, Boston's big question is where the slugging is going to come from.

Willson Contreras had a great season, clubbing 27 home runs. He led the Red Sox with a .516 slugging percentage. Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela were also quality cogs in the machine, slugging .446 and .442, respectively.

But between Roman Anthony's injury, Trevor Story's injury and Jarren Duran's season-long struggles, this offense was a disappointment overall, just barely averaging one home run per game.

Top prospect Franklin Arias could help solve that problem, but whether he'll be on the Opening Day roster remains to be seen. If they're unsure of the answer there, adding some middle infield pop is a must.

Ten pitchers started at least three games for the Cubs in 2026.

Of that bunch, Jameson Taillon is already long gone. Matthew Boyd has a mutual option that won't be exercised (because they never are). Clay Holmes has a player option that he will almost certainly decline. Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman and David Peterson are unrestricted free agents.

That leaves Edward Cabrera (who was a massive disappointment en route to a 5.96 ERA) and a trio of swingmen in Javier Assad, Ben Brown and Colin Rea.

Now, they do have Justin Steele hopefully returning at full strength in 2027. Cade Horton should be back from his Tommy John surgery somewhere around the All-Star Break. But Cubs president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer already said , "The great majority of our focus is going to be on pitching acquisition."

It'd be a surprise if they are part of the bidding war for Tarik Skubal, but it'd be equally surprising if they don't either re-sign one of their own free agents or end up with someone from that "best available aside from Skubal" tier of Michael King, Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers.

The White Sox led the American League in scoring and will retain 12 of the 13 players who made at least 100 plate appearances.

Needless to say, they'll be focused on pitching.

For better or worse, they do have Luis Castillo making $22.75M next season. If he's healthy, he'll be a starter.

Sean Burke is also a lock to start after his breakout season. Davis Martin presumably lands at No. 3 in the rotation, with Hagen Smith getting stretched out and taking on a bigger role in 2027.

Not exactly an irreplaceable arm out of the bunch, though. The fifth spot is anyone's guess between Anthony Kay, Noah Schultz, Grant Taylor, Tanner McDougal and maybe Shane Smith.

Chicago has money to spend, though. They should be looking to add a frontline starter to increase their World Series odds in their second (and possibly final) season with Munetaka Murakami.

In Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, the Reds are more than fine at both shortstop and first base.

Pick anywhere else in Cincinnati's lineup, though, and there is work to be done.

Their third-most valuable position player is catcher Tyler Stephenson, who is now a free agent. They're also losing 26 home runs from Eugenio Suárez. While JJ Bleday's May breakout was a fun story, he hit .188 with a .626 OPS over his final 90 games—and he's still probably the surest thing in Cincinnati's outfield.

Third base might be the biggest conundrum of all, though.

Ke'Bryan Hayes is still owed a total of $29M over the next four seasons, but he just had one of the worst offensive seasons in MLB history and was nowhere near as great defensively as he has been in the past.

Fortunately, Stewart can also play third base, so any corner infielder would do. But with the right acquisition, the Reds could literally double Hayes' .419 OPS from this past season. That'd be a big first step in the right direction.

Biggest Roster Hole : First Base / Designated Hitter

With José Ramírez struggling through by far his worst season in more than a decade, the lack of potency in Cleveland's lineup was more glaring than ever.

They were the only team that didn't have at least one player hit 23 home runs, led surprisingly by Angel Martínez with 18.

First base was the biggest disappointment, though.

Kyle Manzardo, Rhys Hoskins, Nathaniel Lowe and David Fry each played at least 14 games there. None finished the regular season with an OPS better than .684. (With Cleveland, at any rate. Lowe had an .820 OPS with Cincinnati before the trade deadline.)

They do have Ralphy Velazquez waiting in the wings. He hit .326/.401/.761 with 18 home runs in his final 37 games at Triple-A Columbus this season, but they refused to call him up. Maybe he can bring the big lumber to first base in 2027?

Even if he does, they could still use a right-handed bat at DH. Hoskins was their only player to hit at least nine right-handed home runs in 2026. He most likely will not be back next season.

Biggest Roster Hole : A pitcher worth building around

Over the past six years, there have been 680 cases in which a pitcher posted an ERA of 4.32 or lower while logging at least 30 innings as a starter.

Every single team has had at least 14 such seasons.

Their home-field disadvantage doesn't help matters, of course, but the Rockies also have an MLB-worst 5.22 ERA away from home since the beginning of 2021. They simply never have any pitcher worth starting on Opening Day, let alone further down in the rotation.

Preferably one with at least three years of team control so they can eventually stockpile some talent around him?

Detroit's starting rotation also has some serious question marks, at least in terms of big league experience. Beyond Framber Valdez, Keider Montero is their most established option with 53 career starts. Troy Melton, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan have combined for 49. They may well be Nos. 3-5 in this rotation in 2027.

Jobe was one of the top prospects in all of baseball heading into the 2025 campaign. Melton has been great when healthy. Detroit wanted Ryan in the Tarik Skubal trade for a reason. They aren't household names yet, but it could be a respectable starting five.

What isn't respectable is that the bullpen was largely responsible for one of the "unluckiest" seasons in MLB history.

With a +71 run differential, Detroit should have gone 89-73. Instead, it went 76-86, missing their pythagorean record by a minus-13. It's the first minus-12 or worse since the 1993 Mets went 59-103 for a minus-14.

Blowing 31 saves played a big part in the Tigers' underachievement. Now, they have to decide whether Kenley Jansen is worth a $12M club option. You've got to think they'll be investing in different relievers this winter.

Houston's starting rotation could also use a makeover this offseason.

However, there's a perfect world in which Hunter Brown, Hayden Wesneski and Cristian Javier all stay healthy in 2027, buttressed by another good year from Peter Lambert, a better sophomore season from Tatsuya Imai and maybe Brandon Walter returning from Tommy John surgery and picking up where he left off in August 2025.

Good luck cooking up a similar best-case scenario for a team that started 12 different players in left field and had just two players start at least 50 total games in the outfield—Cam Smith with 139 and Taylor Trammell with 73.

Overall, Houston got a .662 OPS from its outfield, good for second-worst in the majors. That includes 25 games when Yordan Alvarez played left field and had a 1.239 OPS. Taking away those 105 plate appearances plummets them into dead last with a mark of .632.

Maybe they found something late in the year with Lucas Spence at center field, but he had a .237 batting average in 239 games played in the minors and was never regarded as a top prospect.

Basically, they're heading into the offseason to prepare for open auditions for starting roles at both left and center field. Even in right, Smith has a .670 OPS two years into his career and is the lone sure thing in this outfield, pretty much by default.

At the plate, Jac Caglianone had a pretty great second season in the majors, posting the same .834 OPS as Washington's CJ Abrams. However, the former starting pitcher/first baseman is still adjusting to life in right field, posting a minus-9 fielding run value and minus-10 outs above average in 2026.

He's the one player who will definitely be starting in Kansas City's outfield in 2027.

Kyle Isbel and Isaac Collins played a combined 234 games in the outfield this season. They were the definition of replacement-level players, whether you use FanGraphs or Baseball-Reference as your source for that metric.

They kept starting, though, because the other options weren't any more promising.

What else is new for the Royals, though? Isbel in center has been their lone constant in recent years. He's a plus fielder who is consistently ninth in the batting order with a .636 OPS since the beginning of 2022.

They probably can't justify paying the going rate to get Randy Arozarena in free agency, but what a game-changer he could be in left field for an offense that is perpetually sputtering in spite of Bobby Witt Jr.

Biggest Roster Hole : Offense in General

Mike Trout had his healthiest season in a decade, while Zach Neto hit 27 home runs and stole 24 bases, yet the Angels suffered 100 losses for the first time in franchise history, almost ranking dead last in the majors in scoring.

Catcher was the biggest black hole of all their positions, with seven backstops combining for a .550 OPS. However, third base (.610), second base (.620) and right field (.647) weren't much better, as the Halos slugged an MLB-worst .369.

Can they plug enough of those holes to turn things around in Trout's age-35 season?

Or would they be better suited to trading away Neto (and Reid Detmers) in hopes of rebuilding and getting Trout the first postseason win of his career in the final year of his massive contract (2030)?

The latter route seems to be the way to go, especially given the lack of MLB-ready talent in this farm system. They've stubbornly refused to embrace a rebuild over the past half-decade, which is why they're in this mess today.

Everyone knows about the Dodgers' well-compensated star players. With the exception of Tarik Skubal hitting the open market after they rented him for a couple of months, they aren't going to lose any of their big-ticket items.

An underrated factor in this dynastic run has been their glue guys: Utilitymen Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernández, who play anywhere and seem to always deliver at least one huge moment in October, along with middle relievers like Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen and Evan Phillips—the latter of whom has yet to allow a single run in 16.0 career innings in the postseason.

All five are headed to free agency, along with Skubal, while Rojas and Treinen may be preparing to retire.

Can they adequately backfill the spots that open up?

Those are the little things that could become the Dodgers' Achilles' heel, especially as the likes of Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy and Mookie Betts progress deeper into their mid/late 30s.

If Owen Caissie can turn things around after a rough first full season in the majors, Miami's offense has the potential to be pretty good.

Same goes for the starting rotation if Max Meyer (neck) and top prospect Thomas White (shoulder) can bounce back from ending the regular season on the IL.

However, their bullpen situation was far from great. They now have a gaping hole at closer, with Pete Fairbanks and his 6.31 ERA (mercifully) headed to free agency.

Do the Marlins swing big in free agency for Raisel Iglesias or David Bednar?

Or did the $13M whiff on Fairbanks scare them away from once again ponying up eight figures for a reliever?

After posting a positive run differential for the first time since 2010, we'd certainly like to see the Marlins make a real effort to win in their final season with Sandy Alcantara.

Jake Bauers was one of the biggest breakout stars of 2026, more than doubling his previous career high for home runs in a single season (from 12 to 26) while posting an .874 OPS that ranked 10th-best among qualified hitters.

Bauers is also set to become a free agent, as he is surely headed for a nice pay bump after making just $2.7M this season.

Maybe the Brewers find a way to keep him, but they're going to need to do something this offseason about their first-base situation.

Notably, one option could involve a 19-year-old top prospect in all of baseball, Jesús Made. Whether it's moving him, Cooper Pratt or Joey Ortiz to first base, that trio plus Brice Turang could be the best infield in the majors in 2027—if Made is ready for the show.

More likely, though, if they can't re-sign Bauers, they'll roll with Andrew Vaughn as the right-handed half of a 1B platoon, while bringing in a Nathaniel Lowe or Dominic Smith on the cheap for the left-handed half.

Perhaps more so than any other team, the Twins need to decide whether they truly believe they can win the 2027 World Series.

They hope to have Pablo López back from his Tommy John surgery early in the season, but it will be the final year of his contract. That "final year" part is also true for Joe Ryan, Dean Kremer, Bailey Ober, Jeff Hoffman, Trevor Larnach, Victor Caratini and Anthony Banda.

If nothing changes this winter, it's four-fifths of the projected starting rotation, two key relievers and two starting position players.

Do they let it ride? Double down with a big acquisition? Or trade away several of those expiring contracts to lay a stronger foundation for a longer push a couple of years down the road?

Well, if they're in it to win it, adding a catcher to replace the outgoing Ryan Jeffers is a near-must, because Caritini and Alex Jackson are hardly a championship-caliber combination at backstop.

They do have quite the stockpile of catching prospects, but Khadim Diaw is the only one who reasonably could be a factor in 2027.

Maybe they extend Jeffers a one-year qualifying offer, even though it's probably an overpay? That move would be a solid stopgap solution until the next generation of catchers is ready.

Whether Bo Bichette stays with the Mets or opts out is a pretty massive variable in the MLB offseason. If he does leave, they still have Brett Baty, Mark Vientos, Christopher Morel, Jorge Polanco and Ronny Mauricio with hot corner experience in the big leagues, plus Jefferson Rojas as a top prospect who could take those reins as early as next season.

They don't need to do anything about their third-base situation.

Can they honestly justify heading into spring training with Sean Manaea, Kodai Senga, Christian Scott, Zac Thornton, Jonah Tong and Tylor Megill battling to fill out the rotation beyond Nolan McLean?

Scott and Thornton were pleasant surprises as fixtures in the rotation this season, but it's hard to believe they might be the No. 2 and No. 3 starters for a team that spends close to half a billion dollars on payroll (and luxury tax) every year.

They'll be in the mix for Tarik Skubal. They almost have to be. If they don't land him, we'd be shocked if they didn't sign at least one of the top six or seven arms on the market—especially if Bichette opts out.

The Yankees' infield situation feels extra dire after Monday night's errors-laden nightmare, but they enter the offseason with a projected infield alignment of Ben Rice, Anthony Volpe, George Lombard Jr. and Ryan McMahon, plus Luis García Jr. and José Caballero off the bench.

It's not so much "a hole that needs to be filled" as it is "an area where they may look to make a big splash."

With David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Tim Hill among the Yankees' relievers hitting free agency, they've got pretty much nothing but holes in the bullpen.

Re-signing Bednar is surely within the realm of possibility, if not the likeliest outcome for the established closer.

That's merely the first step, though, as Brent Headrick might be the only returnee who was used somewhat regularly in high-leverage situations.

Go get Adrián Morejón or Alex Vesia. Bring back Luke Weaver or Jonathan Loáisiga. Turn this deficiency into a strength, or else prepare to extend what is already this franchise's longest World Series drought in more than a century.

Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Bryson Stott combined for 7.5 bWAR in 2026.

The rest of the Phillies position players combined for a minus-2.1 bWAR.

Trea Turner's fall from grace was the biggest individual contributor to Philadelphia's offensive struggles. In the blink of an eye, he went from a batting champ and MVP candidate in 2025 to one of the most problematic contracts in baseball right now. If 2026 is just his new normal with seven years left on this deal, yikes.

J.T. Realmuto also regressed considerably in his age-35 season. And though Brandon Marsh was awesome in the first half en route to All-Star honors, he had a .482 OPS in his final 73 games played.

For better or worse, those three will be back in 2027. And now the Phillies have to replace some combination of Luis Arraez, Edmundo Sosa and Alec Bohm while trying to address the fact that they had the worst team batting WAR in the majors.

With the eight-man nucleus of Harper, Schwarber, Turner, Realmuto, Zack Wheeler, Aaron Nola, Cristopher Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo slated to make a combined $198M next season—not to mention Stott, Marsh and Jhoan Duran possibly each headed for eight-figure salaries in arbitration—good luck making that happen.

Brandon Lowe had a fantastic season at second base for the Pirates. He wasn't an All-Star, but he might get a down-ballot vote or two for NL MVP for his career-best 152 hits with 35 home runs, 94 runs and 96 RBI.

At any rate, the only other players to put up numbers at least that high in all four categories were Pete Crow-Armstrong, Yordan Alvarez, Junior Caminero and Pete Alonso.

Now he's a free agent, though, so it's back to the drawing board.

The good news for the Pirates—if they're willing to spend some money again—is that there has perhaps never been a better winter to need a second baseman.

In addition to Lowe, there's Jazz Chisholm Jr., Luis Arraez and Gleyber Torres available in free agency. They could also buy low on Ha-Seong Kim or Jonathan India coming off disastrous seasons, or bring utilityman Edmundo Sosa over from the other side of Pennsylvania.

Basically, if they don't enter 2027 with a better plan than Nick Gonzales at second base with Jared Triolo at third base, they've got some explaining to do.

Ten pitchers logged at least 20 innings in a starting role for the Padres in 2026.

Here's where they stand heading into the offseason.

Unrestricted free agents: Walker Buehler, Casey Mize, Robbie Ray

Player option, likely to be declined: Michael King

Mutual options, which never get exercised: Griffin Canning, Lucas Giolito

Made 20 starts at Triple-A with a 7.49 ERA: JP Sears

Should be in San Diego's 2027 rotation: Randy Vásquez, Nick Pivetta (club option)

The Padres did at least finally see Joe Musgrove on a mound again during the postseason after two years away. Maybe he can be their ace next season.

There's also hope that Yu Darvish will return after missing all of 2026—and would do so as possibly the oldest player in the league, unless Max Scherzer comes back again.

But a rotation of Musgrove, Pivetta, Vásquez, Darvish and Sears doesn't inspire a whole lot of confidence.

San Francisco came away from the trade deadline with both Blade Tidwell and Carsen Whisenhunt as key fixtures in the starting rotation, replacing Tyler Mahle and Robbie Ray. In fact, they started for the Giants on the first two days after the deadline.

However, Whisenhunt underwent Tommy John surgery in mid-September, with Tidwell suffering the same fate less than a month later.

They had already lost Trevor McDonald to Tommy John shortly before the deadline, as well as Hayden Birdsong during spring training.

Maybe Birdsong returns around the All-Star Break, but the other three are almost certainly not pitching in 2027.

That leaves the Giants with a projected starting rotation of Logan Webb, Landen Roupp, Adrian Houser and some combination of Anthony Molina, Matt Wilkinson, Yunior Marté and César Perdomo, to be determined in spring training.

Maybe it pans out? Wilkinson, Marté and Perdomo all made their MLB debuts less than two months ago, none of them regarded as anything close to an upper-echelon prospect. But those three and Molina all fared reasonably well in their 25ish innings pitched down the stretch.

Got to think the Giants will be looking to add at least one sure thing to their rotation, though.

Without a close runner-up, Randy Arozarena was Seattle's most valuable player in 2026. He was also the Mariners' only All-Star.

And now that he's a free agent, things are looking especially bleak for an offense that already was a colossal disappointment.

The late-season arrivals of top prospects Michael Arroyo and Lázaro Montes inspired some hope for the future. But how much stock can the M's reasonably put in a pair of guys who both turn 22 within the next month and who have combined for 100 plate appearances in the majors?

As things presently stand, it's looking like those two, Dominic Canzone and Luke Raley as the candidates to fill the LF, RF and DH spots in the Opening Day lineup.

Is there any chance they can re-sign Arozarena?

Or maybe snag either Ian Happ or Seiya Suzuki from the long list of Cubs free agents?

Biggest Roster Hole : Ace-Caliber Starting Pitcher

For a team that was expected to endure at least one more rebuilding year, the Cardinals had a pretty respectable starting rotation.

Matthew Liberatore got roughed up a bit, but Michael McGreevy, Kyle Leahy, Andre Pallante, Quinn Mathews and Hunter Dobbins each made at least eight starts while posting a sub-4.00 ERA. Remove Dobbins from the equation after his Tommy John surgery in September and that's the projected starting rotation heading into the offseason.

Here's a question, though: Had the Cardinals made the postseason, who would they have wanted lined up to start in the wild card round?

Or who should toe the rubber on Opening Day?

They have a nice stockpile of middle-of-the-rotation arms, but they are desperately lacking in the ace department.

Given the way they have operated over the years, we certainly don't expect them to go sign Tarik Skubal, or even one of the potentially $100M arms available beyond that two-time Cy Young recipient.

Could they trade for one year of someone like Sandy Alcantara, Joe Ryan or Logan Gilbert, though?

With the exception of Cedric Mullins' $10M mutual option for 2027, every remotely noteworthy batter will be back for Tampa Bay. And considering the Rays have already been rolling with Jonny DeLuca over Mullins in center field during this postseason run—plus top prospect Theo Gillen possibly in the mix for an Opening Day roster spot—that's not a major loss.

Freddy Peralta is a free agent, though. So is Nick Martinez, once his $20M mutual option becomes a $4M buyout. And in the interest of peeking ahead, the Rays have just one year left on each of Drew Rasmussen, Shane McClanahan, Griffin Jax and Steven Matz.

They should be getting Ryan Pepiot back, though, after he missed all of 2026 to hip surgery.

September call-ups Ty Johnson and Brody Hopkins could also factor into the 2027 rotation, although the latter desperately needs to work on his control, issuing 92 walks, 11 wild pitches and nine hit batsmen in 94 innings pitched at Triple-A Durham.

Even this biggest hole barely feels like a speedbump for the AL's No. 1 seed.

Biggest Roster Hole : Back of the Rotation

The Texas Rangers drafted Jack Leiter No. 2 overall in 2021 and Kumar Rocker No. 3 overall in 2022. Both pitchers made their MLB debut in 2024.

But through a combined 100 appearances in the big leagues, let's just say things haven't gone according to plan.

Rocker had his best/healthiest season yet in 2026 and was a respectable No. 3/4 starter with a 4.38 ERA and 4.31 FIP. He now has a career bWAR of 0.0 .

Leiter had a similarly productive year in 2025, but regressed considerably this season, last pitching in mid-June before an ankle surgery and a subsequent biceps injury. He now has a career bWAR of minus-1.6 .

But it's kind of now or never for the Rangers.

Nathan Eovaldi has one year left on his deal. So does MacKenzie Gore. And though the Rangers have a $20M club option to bring back Jacob deGrom in 2028, he turns 40 that June.

Could they sign an ace-caliber pitcher to a multi-year deal now?

Or are they going to continue budgeting their way right out of this window of opportunity?

Biggest Roster Hole : Left Field / Designated Hitter

If George Springer is hanging up his cleats—they would need to re-sign him as a free agent if he's not—the Blue Jays have one returning player (Kazuma Okamoto) who hit more than 10 home runs this season.

To some extent, they just need to hope for better production (from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Ernie Clement) and better health (from Addison Barger and Anthony Santander) in 2027, but that can't be their entire gameplan for addressing what was the lowest-scoring offense in the majors this season.

As things presently stand, it's looking like Santander, Charles McAdoo and Jonatan Clase sharing the LF/DH duties, at least until Barger returns from his elbow surgery.

And if that doesn't scream "Better go sign Randy Arozarena this winter," pray tell, what does?

If such things concern you, Arozarena does have rather terrible career numbers in Toronto, with just one home run in 34 career games played in Canada. But there are other options like Ian Happ and Joc Pederson available in free agency, not to mention Steven Kwan as a trade candidate.

A lot of the picks for biggest roster hole have been debatable.

The Washington Nationals blew a record-smashing 42 saves in 2026, with two particular collapses from June that the front office should have to rewatch every time they think twice about investing in better arms.

On June 10, the Nationals carried a 9-1 lead into the eighth inning in San Francisco. They gave up five in the eighth and five more in the ninth, as Bryce Eldridge ended the game with a walk-off grand slam.

Not two weeks later on June 23, they led the Phillies 5-3 heading into the eighth. After a bases-loaded double that blew the lead, Jorbit Vivas put them back ahead with a three-run home run in the bottom of the eighth. But after striking out the first two Phillies in the ninth, they allowed 10 consecutive batters to reach base, allowing eight runs in an unthinkable meltdown.

They allowed an MLB-worst 86 runs in the ninth inning and a staggering 124 runs in the eighth inning.

What steps will they take to address that massive shortcoming?

articles.title: The 10 Greatest MLB Divisional Series Upsets in Postseason History
articles.summary: There will be no major upsets in the Division Series round of the 2026 playoffs, so the only way to experience that particular thrill involves diving into history.
articles.body:
There will be no major upsets in the Division Series round of the 2026 playoffs, so the only way to experience that particular thrill involves diving into history.

So, here are the 10 greatest upsets in the history of the ALDS and the NLDS.

Just to be clear, the mismatches in question concern not payroll, but performance. Since 1995, there have been 13 cases of one team beating another in the DS round despite a gap of at least 10 wins between the two during the regular season. In nine of these cases, it was a 100-win team going down.

Our focus along the way will primarily be on the losing teams. It's winners that history remembers, and that's at the expense of teams that, while ultimately disappointing, were favorites for a reason. This is their chance to shine again.

Let's begin with some honorable mentions and then count down the upsets in order from least to most shocking.

1996 ALDS: Baltimore Orioles over Cleveland Indians

Series Result: 4 games, +5 run differential

This was one of those powerhouse teams that Cleveland had in the 1990s, with Jim Thome, Manny Ramirez and Albert Belle each going off for over 30 home runs and 100 RBI in service of a 99-win team. Yet even their offense couldn't keep pace with Baltimore's, which homered nine times and scored 25 runs in four games.

1997 ALDS: Cleveland Indians over New York Yankees

Series Result: 5 games, -3 run differential

A year after losing that series to the Orioles, Cleveland took it out on a Yankees club that won 96 games in defense of its 1996 World Series title. They had five guys get MVP votes, including enough to make Tino Martinez the runner-up to Ken Griffey Jr. But they just couldn't get it done in Games 4 and 5, losing both by one run.

2012 NLDS: St. Louis Cardinals over Washington Nationals

Series Result: 5 games, +16 run differential

It may have been the Cardinals who were the defending World Series champions, but the Nationals had home-field advantage after a 98-win season. And they were poised to win the series, too…until Drew Storen let Daniel Descalso and Pete Kozma get the better of him in a four-run ninth for St. Louis in Game 5.

10. 2023 ALDS: Texas Rangers over Baltimore Orioles

Series Result: 3 games, +10 run differential

The 2023 season was meant to be the proper start of the Orioles' reign as an American League powerhouse.

They won 101 games, largely fueled by an offense for which Adley Rutschman and Gunnar Henderson both got MVP votes. The pitching was more so just solid, but Kyle Bradish was a sneaky ace and Félix Bautista was arguably the best closer in the AL, finishing with 33 saves and a 1.58 ERA.

For their part, the Rangers somewhat backed into the playoffs after losing the AL West on the last day of the season. But they pretty much made a mockery of the Orioles. After winning two tight ones to open the series, the Rangers rode seven innings of one-run ball from Nathan Eovaldi to a 7-1 laugher in Game 3.

9. 2017 ALDS: New York Yankees over Cleveland Indians

Series Result: 5 games, +3 run differential

Yes, there was also an 11-win gap at play when Cleveland went down against Baltimore in the 1996 ALDS. Yet that 1996 team didn't do what the 2017 squad did: win 102 games, including an AL-record 22 in a row.

The 2017 squad continued looking like a wrecking ball in the first two games of the ALDS against the Yankees, winning both at home to take a commanding 2-0 lead in the series. Game 2 was the one in which Francisco Lindor hit the huge grand slam to start a comeback that ended with a Yan Gomes walk-off single in the 13th inning.

Alas, Cleveland ran out of offense after that. They scored just five runs in the final three games of the series, largely due to an absolutely loaded Yankees bullpen. To end Game 5, David Robertson and Aroldis Chapman combined for 4.2 innings of hitless, scoreless relief.

8. 2011 NLDS: St. Louis Cardinals over Philadelphia Phillies

Series Result: 5 games, -2 run differential

In case you're too young to remember, the 2011 Phillies were one of those teams that lived up to seemingly impossible-to-live-up-to hype.

Their starting rotation was anointed before the year as one of the best ever , and Roy Halladay, Cliff Lee and Cole Hamels all made good by topping 200 innings with ERAs in the 2.00s. The rotation as a whole had a 2.86 ERA, which was the engine of a 102-win season.

Yet despite not earning their playoff ticket until Game 162 , the Cardinals split the first four games of the NLDS to set up a Halladay vs. Chris Carpenter showdown in Game 5. Carpenter was simply better, answering Halladay's eight one-run innings with a complete-game, three-hit shutout.

7. 2008 NLDS: Los Angeles Dodgers over Chicago Cubs

Series Result: 3 games, +14 run differential

The 2008 Cubs are hardly counted among the great teams in history, but they are a fun little artifact of 2000s baseball.

This was when they had Alfonso Soriano in his heyday as one of MLB's top stars, as well as the perpetually underrated Aramis Ramírez. Even if they were past their primes, Jim Edmonds and Derrek Lee were also there. The Cubs also had four All-Star hurlers in Ryan Dempster, Carlos Zambrando, Kerry Wood and Carlos Mármol.

Yet even if that year's Dodgers were only an 84-win team, they changed for the better after Manny Ramirez arrived and got "Mannywood" up and running. He fueled a 30-23 finish with a 1.232 OPS and 17 home runs down the stretch, and kept it up in the NLDS by going 5-for-10 with two homers and four walks.

6. 2003 NLDS: Chicago Cubs over Atlanta Braves

Series Result: 5 games, +4 run differential

To look back at the 2003 Braves is to gaze in awe at a 101-win team that seemingly had it all.

Tom Glavine was gone, but Greg Maddux was still there and his co-ace, Russ Ortiz, even finished fourth in the NL Cy Young Award voting. They also had John Smoltz closing games to the tune of a 1.12 ERA. Oh , and Chipper Jones, Andruw Jones, Gary Sheffield and Javy López coming off 100-RBI seasons.

As for the Cubs, well, they had Kerry Wood and Mark Prior. That proved to be all that mattered, as they recorded all three of the Cubs' wins in the NLDS and allowed just four earned runs over 24.1 innings as they did so.

5. 2019 NLDS: Washington Nationals over Los Angeles Dodgers

Series Result: 5 games, -1 run differential

The 2019 Dodgers were, at least to that point, probably the best regular season team the franchise had ever known.

They were the first Dodgers squad to win as many as 106 games, and they did so with a +273 run differential that still ranks among the 20 best of all time. Cody Bellinger was the eventual NL MVP, and Clayton Kershaw, Walker Buehler and Hyun-Jin Ryu all got Cy Young Award votes.

It just didn't feel like the Nationals had any business beating those Dodgers, and their fate seemed certain when Kershaw came on to protect a 3-1 lead in the eighth inning of Game 5. But you know the rest: Anthony Rendon and Juan Soto for the tie , and Howie Kendrick for the win .

4. 2022 NLDS: Philadelphia Phillies over Atlanta Braves

Series Result: 4 games, +11 run differential

The 2022 Braves were both a post-championship team and a post-Freddie Freeman team, and it really did feel like the dawn of a new era.

In Freeman's shoes, Matt Olson arrived and recorded 34 homers and 103 RBI. Michael Harris II and Spencer Strider finished first and second in the NL Rookie of the Year voting. Kyle Wright ripped off a 21-win season in support of Max Fried. It was otherwise more of the same from Dansby Swanson and Austin Riley as Ronald Acuña Jr. got his legs back under him following a season-ending ACL tear in 2021.

As for how this 101-win team got pantsed by an 87-win Phillies team in the NLDS, it was largely a case of the bats not having it. Multiple Phillies got hot all at the same time, and none more so than Bryce Harper. He had a 1.592 OPS in the series, and it wasn't even the best thing he did that October.

3. 2023 NLDS: Philadelphia Phillies over Atlanta Braves

Series Result: 4 games, +12 run differential

If the 2022 Braves merely heralded a new era, the 2023 Braves were the team that seemed to usher it in.

The 104 wins were just the start of it. There was also the offense that truly earned comparisons to the 1927 Yankees. It had a collective 123 wRC+, the highest in AL/NL history. This was the 40-70 year for Ronald Acuña Jr., and he didn't even lead the team in homers because of Matt Olson's 54. On the other side of the ball, Spencer Strider won 20 games and led MLB with 281 strikeouts.

And yet, the Phillies just absolutely crushed them in the NLDS. There's just no other way to put it when it's a .937 OPS vs. a .519 OPS. The Phillies homered 11 times in the four games, with Nick Castellanos (4), Bryce Harper (3) and Trea Turner (2) all providing multiples.

2. 2023 NLDS: Arizona Diamondbacks over Los Angeles Dodgers

Series Result: 3 games, +13 run differential

It was the Braves who were the talk of baseball in 2023, yet they were one of two 100-win teams in the National League. The other was this Dodgers squad.

They may not have had Atlanta's offense, but this was the year that Mookie Betts fell one homer short of 40 amid an 8.6-WAR season. Max Muncy and J.D. Martinez also topped 30 homers, while Freddie Freeman added 59 doubles to go with his 29 homers. It was all more than enough to carry a pitching staff that spent much of the season toeing the line between bending and breaking.

At least, that is, until an 84-win Diamondbacks squad pummeled Dodgers pitchers for 19 runs in three games in the NLDS. Most of those (11, to be exact) came in a Game 1 romp at the expense of Clayton Kershaw, which pretty much set the tone for the whole series.

1. 2022 NLDS: San Diego Padres over Los Angeles Dodgers

Series Result: 4 games, +3 run differential

By any reasonable measure, the 2022 Dodgers were an all-time great team. Only they and four others have won as many as 111 games in a season. They're the only one to also do so with a +334 run differential.

This was the year that the Dodgers could do no wrong on the mound. The team had a 2.80 ERA, fueled by four starters who took at least 20 turns and finished with an ERA in the 2.00s. They scored 40 more runs than the next-best team, with Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Trea Turner all posting 5+ WAR.

It should have been the Padres who ran into a buzz saw, but it turned out they had a trump card that was worth more than anything the Dodgers had: their bullpen. It handled 16.0 innings in the NLDS and allowed just one run, whereas Dodgers relievers gave up eight runs and were stuck with two of their three losses.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Guardians force Game 5 after going down 0-2 in ALDS, continuing 120-year drought for White Sox
articles.summary: This series is heading back to Cleveland.
articles.body: The Chicago White Sox welcomed the Cleveland Guardians to the South Side this week with a 2-0 lead in the ALDS and a funny workout playlist featuring songs such as "End of the Road" by Boyz II Men.No one's laughing now.For a second straight game, the Guardians rode an offensive outburst to a road win on Thursday, this time posting a 9-5 victory in Game 4. The series is now tied 2-2 and headed back to Cleveland, with the Guardians on the verge of becoming the first team since the 2017 New York Yankees to erase a 2-0 lead in a division series.Game 5 is scheduled for 8 p.m. ET Saturday, with both starting pitchers TBA as of Thursday evening. The Tampa Bay Rays await the winner in the ALCS.At the very least, the Guardians' win means one of MLB's odder droughts will continue. The White Sox haven't clinched a playoff series at home since they won their first title in the 1906 World Series, a span of 120 years that includes 11 trips to the postseason. That was 10 popes ago.Game 4 had been shaping up to be delightfully chaotic, with a pair of lead changes in the fifth inning alone, but all of that turned out to be setup for a knockout punch from Cleveland in the sixth. A slow-motion disaster for Chicago began with a hit-by-pitch and steal for Angel Martínez, then an RBI double from Travis Bazzana to tie the game 4-4.The White Sox knew the risks of allowing the rally to continue, so they made the natural choice. They brought in relief ace Grant Taylor. But sometimes the obvious move just doesn't work out.Taylor, who posted a 2.25 ERA in the regular season and didn't allow an earned run in his first three multi-inning postseason appearances, faced six Cleveland batters and didn't get a single out. Jo Adell makes it a SIX-run inning for the Guardians! pic.twitter.com/dIVeEDZ8xc— MLB (@MLB) October 9, 2026 The game unraveled for Chicago with every baserunner, going Patrick Bailey single, Brayan Rocchio walk, Steven Kwan walk, José Ramírez single, Chase DeLauter single, Jo Adell single. By the time the White Sox mercifully pulled Taylor for Bryan Hudson, it was a 9-4 game at a stunned Rate Field.It was a messy game up and down for a Chicago pitching staff that used Hagen Smith as an opener and Erick Fedde as the bulk guy behind him. The unit walked seven and hit one batter against only three strikeouts. All the Guardians had to do was be patient, though they also got their first two homers of the postseason from Bailey and Ramírez in the fifth inning.PATRICK BAILEY!Guardians take the lead again! pic.twitter.com/moTngem8i5— MLB (@MLB) October 9, 2026 The one consolation for Chicago is that the Guardians felt the need to bring in Gavin Williams for the ninth inning after Cade Smith surrendered a home run and walk to begin the ninth. It was Williams' first career relief appearance, two days before he is expected to start Game 5 in Cleveland.

articles.title: MLB Free Agents 2026 Rumors and Updated Landing-Spot Predictions
articles.summary: The MLB hot stove is starting to heat up.
articles.body:
The MLB hot stove is starting to heat up.

With fewer teams remaining in the World Series chase and more shifting into offseason mode, there are starting to be some rumblings around the top free agents in this class.

Let's dive into the discussions, then, with a rumor roundup and updated landing-spot predictions.

Padres, Ty France Hoping to Run It Back?

Back with his first ever MLB employer, the San Diego Padres, and inside of his home state of California, Ty France engineered a stars-all-aligned kind of campaign. The 31-year-old posted his most wins above replacement to date ( 4.5 ) and set personal-bests in home runs (21) and OPS (.865).

Given how fruitful this partnership proved, it's hardly surprising to hear there is "mutual interest" between the Padres and France, per The Athletic's Dennis Lin .

That said, Lin noted the Padres "have multiple holes to fill in their starting rotation," so France may not be their first priority. And the veteran first baseman admitted "I...understand it's a business."

If France is forced to look elsewhere, he shouldn't have trouble identifying suitors. He has previously earned both All-Star and Gold Glove honors, and again, he was arguably at his best this season.

Landing spots: Houston Astros, New York Mets, San Diego Padres

Amid all of the uncertainty with this offseason, there is one guarantee: Someone is going to pay Tarik Skubal an absurd amount of money. And insiders see two clear candidates regarding whom that someone might be.

"Most insiders project the Dodgers and Mets to be serious bidders," ESPN's Kiley McDaniel reported, "but there is some hesitation surrounding the Dodgers given the controversy around the team's ownership. Some thought the Mets might be looking to do a shorter-term deal such as they did with Bo Bichette, which might not work if Skubal is looking to set a record for guaranteed money."

McDaniel's article, built around discussions with industry insiders, actually listed seven possible landing spots for Skubal. The Detroit Tigers joined the Dodgers and the Mets in the "True contenders" tier, with the New York Yankees mentioned as being "just behind that lead group in total mentions." The Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and San Diego Padres were all brought up as sleepers.

With Skubal being a two-time Cy Young winner and a Scott Boras client, he'll command a payday so rich that it prices out a lot of interested teams. That probably puts Skubal with a marquee team in a marquee market, though a return to Detroit—where he spent his first six-plus MLB seasons—could be compelling.

Landing spots: Detroit Tigers, Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Mets

This marked the second full season for Jazz Chisholm Jr. with the New York Yankees, a relationship first forged ahead of the 2024 deadline. The two-time All-Star is hoping to extend his stay with the Pinstripes.

"I do hope to be back," he told reporters after New York's season-ending loss to the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday.

It'll be interesting to see if that interest is recipocrated from the Yankees' side, and if it is, to what degree. Chisholm had an up-and-down tenure with the team, and he wasn't great with the bat or the glove this postseason. Amid those struggles, he was benched twice in favor of Anthony Volpe.

If Chisholm looked elsewhere, he shouldn't have trouble finding interested suitors. Even with the inconsistency, he amassed 50 homers and 72 steals since the start of the 2025 season, and since he'll only turn 29 in February, he could have more prime years ahead of him.

Landing spots: Los Angeles Angels, San Diego Padres, Toronto Blue Jays
