articles.title: What went wrong for the 2026 Yankees? And where do they go from here?
articles.summary: For the third year in a row, Aaron Judge and Co. watched an opponent celebrate on their field in October.
articles.body:
For the third year in a row, the New York Yankees ended their season by watching an opponent celebrate on the Yankee Stadium grass in October.

On Wednesday, it was the Tampa Bay Rays' turn to do the honors after sweeping New York out of the playoffs , following the Toronto Blue Jays' dominant effort in last year's ALDS and the Los Angeles Dodgers' wrapping things up in five games in the 2025 World Series.

In the ALDS sweep by Tampa, the Yankees' pitching staff generally did its job, just as it had all season. But without Aaron Judge, sidelined due to a calf strain suffered in late September, the Yankees' offense reverted to the worst version of itself — the version that was on display sans Judge for much of the regular season. Only Ben Rice looked remotely locked in, with the rest of the hitters showing minimal resistance to Tampa Bay's army of arms, who flummoxed New York's bats no matter how manager Aaron Boone arranged the lineup. The Yankees struck out 31 times and mustered just 12 hits across the three games, the lowest total in a multigame postseason series in franchise history.

The end of Game 3 was a fitting finale for the "run-it-back" Yankees, a not-so-flattering moniker ascribed after New York spent last offseason going to great lengths to keep its roster largely intact despite the early postseason exit at the hands of Toronto. Last winter featured the retention of outfielder Trent Grisham via the qualifying offer, the re-signing of key role players Amed Rosario and Paul Goldschmidt, plus relievers Paul Blackburn and Ryan Yarbrough, and a massive new contract for outfielder Cody Bellinger — all while making minimal upgrades beyond the returnees.

Across the regular season, some holdovers performed better than others. Blackburn excelled in relief, exemplifying New York's developmental competence and ingenuity on the mound. The veteran Goldschmidt raked in the first half but faded badly down the stretch. Bellinger shined all summer but was a nonfactor against Tampa Bay, going 1-for-12. And after an underwhelming regular season, it was Grisham who represented the Yankees' last hope in the ninth inning of Game 3, having been inserted into the leadoff spot as a last-gasp lineup shake-up from Boone, with hope that his plate discipline could show up when his team needed him most. Instead, with the tying run on second base, Grisham struck out on four pitches, leaving Rice on deck and punctuating an 0-for-5 with three strikeouts.

Fair or not, the optics of the final at-bat of the 2026 Yankees' season make it tough to believe that running it back was ever going to be a recipe for success. Now New York once again begins its offseason in early October with a chance to enact significant change. Early reports indicate that neither general manager Brian Cashman nor manager Aaron Boone is at risk of losing his job, so the roster will be the focus.

Will they shake things up to a meaningful degree? Grisham is one of several key Yankees scheduled to hit free agency , and he appears the least likely to stick around, especially given the emergence of outfielder Spencer Jones. Joining Grisham on the open market will be second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. and closer David Bednar, each of whom could command a significant sum in a notably weak free-agent class. Bednar was a brilliant fit at the backend of Boone's bullpen this year, but the Yankees have proven capable of covering high-leverage innings without paying top dollar. They let Devin Williams and Luke Weaver depart in free agency last year; will they do the same with Bednar?

Chisholm's fit with New York moving forward is more complicated. The Yankees' infield is both completely unsettled and awfully crowded. Is George Lombard Jr. a lock to be the Opening Day shortstop? Could Anthony Volpe be the every-day second or third baseman, or should he be in a bench role? Does Ryan McMahon, still owed $16 million next season, have a place on this roster? And what about midseason addition Luis Garcia Jr. — could he return to his native second base, despite his poor defensive reputation?

And that's just the infield. Giancarlo Stanton has a year remaining on his contract, but his durability is tenuous to say the least, and the DH spot will already be occupied by the likes of Garcia, Rice and perhaps Judge.

As they look to 2027, the Yankees can at least take solace in the knowledge that their pitching staff is in sterling shape, with an excellent (albeit expensive) rotation headlined by an ascendent homegrown ace in Cam Schlittler. Still, there is much to be resolved with their defensive alignment and lineup construction.

Of course, the entire operation still revolves around Judge, whose absence cannot be overlooked when assessing this Yankees season. But as he approaches his 35th birthday in April, Judge's injury-ravaged season is a reminder that his spectacular prime could already be behind him . At the very least, a stronger supporting cast is necessary for him to achieve his ultimate goal of bringing a World Series to the Bronx.

When Judge addressed the media a year ago as the Blue Jays partied in the Bronx, he had undoubtedly done his part in October, hitting .500 across seven postseason games, including a stadium-shaking, three-run homer in New York's Game 3 victory against Toronto. In 2024, Judge was at the center of the collective letdown , having hit just .184 during New York's postseason run and contributed one of the crucial errors in the fifth-inning defensive disaster in World Series Game 5.

This year, for the first time, Judge had to speak about a postseason in which he did not participate. This was also his least successful regular season as a big leaguer; his .871 OPS and 66 games played are both career-low marks in a full season. Injuries were the culprit; a rib fracture cost him three months, and a calf strain rendered him unavailable for the first two rounds of the postseason . It's unclear if Judge would have been activated had the Yankees advanced, but the Rays rendered that what-if moot. Judge, the ultimate main character during this era of Yankees baseball, was relegated to looming large in the background.

That doesn't make his words carry any less weight.

Among a deluge of predictable post-elimination platitudes, these words uttered by the captain and three-time AL MVP in the wake of the Yankees' latest postseason exit stood out. Judge had been asked what he hopes to see from ownership and the front office in response to the franchise once again failing to accomplish its annual goal of winning it all.

"We're the Yankees. I feel like they should go all-in and do what they need to do," Judge said. "That's why I signed back here to play with the Yankees: To fight for a championship every single year. To go all-in. That's what I do every offseason, to get ready to give this team and this city everything we've got. I expect them to do the same."

The intended sentiment is clear. It's not just that the Yankees are dismayed after bowing out of the postseason early in October. It's that this latest collection of Bronx Bombers has fallen well short of the singular standard of this franchise, based on its unrivaled history of being the last team standing.

Sure, the 2026 Yankees delivered their 34th consecutive winning season, the second-longest such streak in major-league history, behind a 39-year streak achieved by the Yankees from 1926 to 1964. The front office, helmed by Brian Cashman since 1998, has annually constructed ballclubs that reside at or near the top of the regular-season standings.

"But that's not good enough here in New York," Judge added. "We're the Yankees. You have to go out there and expect championships and go all-in every year."

They're the Yankees. They're different. They're supposed to win it all.

In the first half of Cashman's nearly three-decade tenure leading New York's baseball operations, the Yankees won four World Series titles (1998, 1999, 2000, 2009), lost in the Fall Classic two other times (2001, 2003) and missed the postseason just once (2008). This is the standard that Judge and his fellow disappointed teammates grew up on. Those who become Yankees tend to embrace the franchise's World Series-forward identity and aspire to uphold its tradition of winning.

But more recently, the Yankees have struggled to recapture the consistent excellence achieved by the previous generation. Over the past 14 seasons, New York has reached one World Series (2025) and missed October altogether on four occasions (2013, 2014, 2016, 2023). Since the Yankees last won the World Series in 2009, 10 different franchises have become champions, including their biggest rivals, the Boston Red Sox, twice.

So yes, they're the Yankees. They still wear pinstripes and have a lot of terrific ballplayers.

But whenever they do finally break through and win it all, there's a good chance they will be exceeding expectations — not fulfilling them.

articles.title: Dodgers vs. Brewers NLCS preview: Have Jackson Chourio and Co. leveled up enough to take down Shohei Ohtani and the Dodgers?
articles.summary: It’s a Dodgers vs. Brewers rematch with a trip to the World Series on the line. Let’s break it down.
articles.body:
We've said goodbye to the Phillies and Cubs, and then to the Braves and Padres. What does that leave? The No. 1 and No. 2 seeds in the National League in a rematch of last year's championship series.

It's Dodgers vs. Brewers with a trip to the World Series on the line. Let's break it down.

Dodgers: L.A.'s star-studded rotation carried the day against Atlanta in the NLDS, with a 1.69 ERA in 21 ⅓ innings of work. Tarik Skubal (Game 1) and Yoshinobu Yamamoto (Game 3) were sensational. Tyler Glasnow (Game 4) was erratic but effective. Only Blake Snell (3 ⅔ innings in Game 2) disappointed. An aging Dodgers offense did enough to support the pitching staff, thanks to timely long balls from veterans Kiké Hernández, Freddie Freeman and Max Muncy. It wasn't an emphatic, resounding performance by any means, but the Dodgers got the job done in Round 1 of their three-peat quest.

Brewers: Milwaukee snapped a 12-game postseason road losing streak with its Game 4 NLDS-clinching win at Petco Park . That might be yet another sign that this Brewers team is for real, ready to reach the World Series for just the second time in franchise history and first since 1982. Run prevention, as always, won the day for Milwaukee against San Diego, with a sparkling 2.5 runs allowed per game. That came in spite of an uncharacteristically shaky defensive display — the Brewers made five errors across the four games. It wasn't exactly a dominant showing from the offense, either, but Milwaukee's lineup kept the line moving and caused enough chaos to dispatch the Padres in a hard-fought series.

This duo went a dismal 3-for-29 with 11 strikeouts and zero extra-base hits against the Braves. Yet somehow, Smith and Ohtani looked even worse than that combined line. It's difficult to envision the Dodgers moving on if these two crucial cogs continue to struggle to that extent.

Ohtani, surely, is playing at less than 100 percent, having never fully recovered from the litany of late-season ailments that pushed him to the IL for the first time in his Dodgers career. He looks skittish, uncertain and uncomfortable at the plate. That's precipitating uncharacteristically questionable swing decisions, which, in turn, are putting him in bad counts and leading to bad outcomes. The four-time MVP is still capable of brilliance — he's less than a year removed from the greatest single-game performance of all time in NLCS Game 4 — but that magic feels less likely from this reduced version of Ohtani.

Smith is a more bizarre story. He missed nearly three months during the regular season but came back on Sept. 1 and looked like his best self for much of the final month (.948 September OPS). But his swing mechanics — at their best, the epitome of do-simple-perfect — are completely out of whack right now. He's still providing oodles of value with his presence behind the plate, but this is not the game-changing offensive force who clocked the World Series-winning blast last year .

The 22-year-old had just three hits in Milwaukee's NLDS victory, but all three came in massive moments. There was the game-tying, two-run homer off Robbie Ray in Game 1 , the walk-off single against Mason Miller in Game 2 and the go-ahead, laser-beam single in Game 4. But while that timeliness is wonderful, a bit more production from Chourio feels like the easiest way for Milwaukee's offense to level up against the Dodgers. He's easily the most talented Brewers hitter and already the franchise's all-time postseason home run leader. Last year, Chourio blasted Milwaukee's only long ball against L.A. in the NLCS and was one of two Brewers with at least three hits in that series. For a team to go deep in October, special players need to do special things. There might not be a more special talent on the field (besides a healthy Ohtani) than this guy.

Dodgers: Starting pitching + something else

The Dodgers' rotation, at this point, feels as reliable as any unit in the sport. But if L.A.'s offense continues to underwhelm, that might be enough. They need either (1) a few more hitters to step up, (2) a total lockdown showing from the bullpen or (3) near-perfection from the already brilliant rotation. Option No. 1 is easily the likeliest path to victory. The Dodgers have so many talented, October-proven bats that it feels inevitable that one or more of Ohtani, Smith, Teoscar Hernández, Mookie Betts or Andy Pages will catch fire. How many do and to what extent will likely determine whether the Dodgers reach the World Series for the third straight year. But Option No. 2 is a possibility as well. Or, if Skubal and Yamamoto both dominate in both of their starts, that might be enough.

In the 2025 regular season, Milwaukee had MLB's lowest chase rate at 25.5%. But in their NLCS capitulation against the Dodgers, that number skyrocketed to 34.5%. Come October, some jump in chase rate is expected; the best pitchers are throwing harder and more often. Still, that's an unsustainably high spike, and it sank the Brewers' offense.

This regular season, the Brewers once again led the sport in chase rate at 26.8%, setting up an unstoppable force against an immovable object in the NLCS. Los Angeles' pitching staff ranked first in chase rate at 33.1%. Skubal, Snell and Yamamoto all ranked in the 85th percentile.

Laying off pitches outside the strike zone, particularly early in counts, would be a total game-changer for this low-power Brewers offense. Doing so would force Dodgers hurlers into hitter's counts, run pitch counts higher and bring the bullpen in play earlier. That's when damage happens. Jake Bauers, Garrett Mitchell, Andrew Vaughn, Christian Yelich, Sal Frelick and Brice Turang were all 20th percentile in chase rat. They'll need to keep that going. And Milwaukee's most swing-happy character, Chourio, has to stay disciplined.

In the NLDS, Los Angeles used Snell in Game 2 and Yamamoto in Game 3, but they're likely to swap those two for the NLCS. That decision could have an interesting trickle-down effect if Snell and Glasnow can't work deep in games. Splitting up Snell and Glasnow against Atlanta meant that Los Angeles' bullpen wouldn't need to cover a multitude of innings on back-to-back days. But with Skubal and Yamamoto lined up for two starts each in his series, the Dodgers won't have that luxury this time around. Getting any semblance of length from Snell could be critical.

The 2025 Brewers looked completely overmatched against the Los Angeles pitching staff throughout that brief NLCS. But while their lineup is markedly better this go-around, Milwaukee's offense still operates with that same high-contact, low-power style. That strategy worked well enough against a good, not great, Padres staff, but this Dodgers group is a different beast. Milwaukee's run prevention apparatus, at this point, has proven itself capable of keeping scores low and games close, no matter who's on the mound. But the Brewers can't win ballgames 0-0.

Last year, Milwaukee's offense was helpless against Los Angeles' pitching staff, while the Ohtani-led Dodgers lineup hummed against the Brewers' arms. But this aging Dodgers position-player group looks shakier than ever, and the Brewers' bats have all leveled up. To win the series, Milwaukee will need to win at least one game started by Skubal or Yamamoto. That's a tough task, but I think they're up for the fight and that Chourio has enough pixie dust to knock off baseball's big, bad juggernaut in what should be an unforgettable battle.

articles.title: Gavin Williams closed out Game 4 of ALDS. He's also starting Guardians-White Sox rubber match
articles.summary: Williams made his first professional appearance out of the bullpen on Thursday night in Chicago, relieving Cleveland closer Cade Smith to seal a 9-5 victory.
articles.body:
Before Thursday night, Gavin Williams hadn't registered a relief appearance in his professional career. The 27-year-old right-handed ace was called upon to shut down a last-ditch effort from the Chicago White Sox in Game 4 of the American League Division Series.

Williams relieved closer Cade Smith, who gave up a solo shot and a walk to start the bottom of the ninth inning after spinning a scoreless frame in the eighth after two shutout innings the previous day in a Game 3 Cleveland victory.

Although Williams conceded a single to the first Chicago batter he faced, he regrouped and dashed the hopes of the South Siders, swiftly ending a potential comeback bid and extending the White Sox's 120-year drought without a postseason series-clinching win at home. Williams sealed the 9-5 decision, the Guardians' second consecutive road triumph after beginning the ALDS with back-to-back defeats.

Two days later, the 6-foot-6, 250-pound hurler will have to come up big for the Guardians again, as he's remaining the team's pick to start a winner-take-all Game 5 against the White Sox. Williams, this season's AL strikeout leader , will get the nod with a chance to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL Championship Series on the line in Cleveland.

"It's a Game 5, win or go home," Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said Friday, per MLB.com . "Gavin wants the ball. We want him to have the ball, and it's his game."

Granted, Thursday was a scheduled throw day for Williams anyway, but his emergency relief appearance made for an unorthodox between-starts bullpen session. Game 4 saw Guardians left-handed starter Parker Messick last just 2 1/3 innings. Vogt had to go to his bullpen early. And, ultimately, he needed more help to wrap things up after Smith's fatigue seemed to show in the ninth.

Fortunately for Cleveland, Williams managed to keep his pitch count relatively low, needing only 18 pitches to record three outs and finish out the series-extending win. He also started Game 2 of the ALDS on Monday, dazzling with 11 punchouts . That said, in a 4-3 loss, he allowed three walks and four hits and was accountable for two runs across five innings of work.

The upstart White Sox have embraced unconventional pitching plans throughout their feel-good postseason run. But on Saturday, they'll be handing the ball to right-handed starter Sean Burke.

Burke, like Williams, also pitched in Game 2. He entered that matchup during the third inning and went 5 1/3 innings, surrendering one hit, one walk and one earned run while logging six K's.

The White Sox used seven pitchers in their Game 4 loss, including closer Grant Taylor. The righty was roughed up in a doomed sixth inning that consisted of six Guardians runs.

A day of rest is helpful for both teams' pitching staffs. The White Sox narrowly edged the Guardians in the regular-season series, 7-6; however, Cleveland wound up wearing the AL Central crown.

The division foes are taking the ALDS down to the wire, too, with Williams and Burke getting the first stab at the showdown on the mound.

articles.title: New Yankees Rumors on Aaron Boone's Hot Seat as Manager After MLB Playoff Exit to Rays
articles.summary: The New York Yankees aren't expected to part ways with manager Aaron Boone after falling to the Tampa Bay Rays in their American League Division Series matchup, according to Jon Heyman of the New York Post.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees aren't expected to part ways with manager Aaron Boone after falling to the Tampa Bay Rays in their American League Division Series matchup, according to Jon Heyman of the New York Post .

"I don't expect them to move on," Heyman reported (0:58 mark). "I think he'll be back. He's got a year to go. We've got the lockout coming. Too many reasons for them to keep him, it'd be a lot easier."

The 10 Greatest MLB Divisional Series Upsets 😮

Boone owns a 790-565 overall record during his tenure with the Yankees, but the team hasn't experienced consistent success in the postseason.

New York has made the playoffs in eight of his nine years as manager, although it hasn't won a World Series title over that span. The Yankees captured one AL pennant in 2024 before they lost the Fall Classic in five games at the hands of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Even though it's worth noting that New York was without star Aaron Judge during its latest playoff run, the team still scored just five total runs across three games while getting swept by the Rays in the ALDS.

That doesn't necessarily mean a change will be coming at manager, though.
